The Persistence of Small Joys

There's a particular quality to morning light in late autumn that I've never been able to name properly. It arrives sideways, somehow, having lost the summer's vertical confidence. It stretches across kitchen tables and catches dust motes that you didn't notice were there, making the ordinary air suddenly visible, suddenly theatrical. I find myself stopping mid-coffee sometimes, arrested by this nothing-special moment, this light doing what light has done for millennia without my attention or approval.

I've been thinking about attention lately, about how we spend it like a currency we don't realize is finite. The world has become a slot machine of stimuli, each pull promising the jackpot of engagement, and we stand there feeding it our hours, our capacity for presence, while somewhere outside the casino the autumn light performs its quiet spectacle for no audience at all. I don't mean this as a complaint against modernity—I'm as tethered to my devices as anyone, perhaps more so. I mean it as a kind of puzzlement, a wondering about what we lose and what we might recover.

Last spring I started walking the same three-mile loop through my neighborhood every morning, not for exercise or any virtuous reason, but because I'd run out of podcasts and found myself, for the first time in years, alone with my own thoughts. The first week was uncomfortable in a way that surprised me. I kept reaching for my phone, checking for messages that weren't there, manufacturing urgency where none existed. But by the second week, something shifted. I began to notice that one house had a magnolia tree that bloomed two weeks before all the others on the street. I learned which dogs would bark behind which fences, which ones would wag their entire bodies at the fence slats hoping for a hand to scratch through. I found a spot where, if the wind was right, you could smell the bakery three blocks away, that particular yeasty warmth that no candle has ever successfully replicated.

The loop became a kind of meditation without the formal structure, a way of being present that didn't require an app to guide my breathing or a teacher to correct my posture. I was simply there, walking, noticing. The thoughts that came were not profound. They were the ordinary churn of a mind left to its own devices: memories surfacing unbidden, half-formed ideas for projects I'd never start, imaginary conversations with people I hadn't spoken to in years. But there was something restorative in this unremarkable mental weather, something that the optimized, curated versions of my thinking—when I was producing, performing, communicating—never quite provided.

I think often about a conversation I had with my grandmother shortly before she died. She was ninety-three and had begun to lose words, which for a woman who had always been precise in her language was a particular cruelty. We were sitting in her living room, the one with the heavy velvet curtains that always smelled slightly of cigarettes despite her having quit decades before, and I asked her if she was scared. She looked at me for a long moment, her eyes the pale blue they'd always been, and said, "No, but I'm surprised. I didn't expect to still be interested." She explained that she'd thought old age would be a kind of closing down, a gradual withdrawal from the world, but instead she found herself still curious, still noticing, still wanting to know how things would turn out for people she'd never meet. "It's inconvenient," she said, and laughed, and I understood that she meant the persistence of her own consciousness, its refusal to dim and simplify according to the stories we tell about aging.

That phrase has stayed with me: "I didn't expect to still be interested." Interest, it seems to me now, is a form of love. Not the grand passion kind, but the steady, renewable attention that keeps us connected to the world beyond our own skin. To be interested in the magnolia that blooms early, in the particular gait of a stranger, in the way your friend's voice changes when she talks about her daughter—these are small devotions, but they accumulate. They form a kind of counterweight to the solipsism that threatens any life, the gravity pull of self that makes everything orbit our own needs and narratives.

I've been trying to cultivate this interest more deliberately, to resist the contraction that stress and busyness encourage. It's not easy. The world offers endless justifications for turning inward, for narrowing our circle of concern until it includes only the immediate emergency, the pressing deadline, the familiar face. And there are seasons for this narrowing, times when survival requires a kind of triage. But I'm suspicious of making a permanent home there, of coming to believe that the small curiosities are luxuries we can't afford. They may be the only things we can truly afford, the ones that cost nothing and pay out in ways that don't register on any balance sheet.

The other day I saw a man on the bus trying to teach his young son how to tie a shoe. The boy was perhaps four, his face screwed up in concentration, his small fingers fumbling with the laces. The father was patient in a way that seemed almost supernatural to me, going through the steps again and again, never taking the laces to do it himself, never showing frustration at the repetition. I watched them for twenty minutes, my own stop long past, and when the boy finally managed a lopsided knot that would surely untie within steps, his face opened into a joy so pure it made my throat hurt. The father high-fived him with the gravity of a championship moment. Nobody else on the bus seemed to notice. They were in their phones, their headphones, their own heads.

I don't know what to make of moments like this, whether they mean anything or are simply the random data of being alive in a world full of other people being alive. But I find myself collecting them, these small scenes of ordinary grace, the way you might collect stones on a beach without knowing what you'll do with them. They don't solve anything. They don't make the larger problems of existence any less pressing or real. But they complicate the narrative of decline, of isolation, of a world grown irredeemable. They suggest that alongside whatever catastrophe is unfolding, there is also this: a father teaching a child to tie a shoe, the autumn light making dust motes visible, an old woman surprised to find herself still interested.

The loop continues. I walk it still, most mornings, though now the magnolia has lost its leaves and the bakery's warmth is more welcome than before. The dogs still bark, still wag. My thoughts still churn in their unremarkable way. And somewhere, I trust, the light is arriving sideways, making visible what we otherwise might not see, asking nothing of us but our attention, our small and renewable devotion.
